utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm aware of the housekeeping issues that arose yesterday. Can we deal with them at the end of the day, or at the end of this witness, if we can finish him today?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's -- of course, as the Trial Chamber wishes. However, we anticipate that the direct examination of this witness will be completed in approximately two sessions today. So the issue that we raised yesterday about asking that the Defence predict how long the cross-examination will be at the beginning of the cross-examination would arise then today with this witness. So we would ask, if it's possible, that it could be addressed before that happens, that we would appreciate it. I have also another matter which I wanted to address briefly with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we then deal with this issue and all other matters at the end of -- can I say the end of the examination-in-chief of this witness? We can't do that. He'll be sitting here at that time. Okay. So maybe the best thing is to deal with them right away now. Okay. Let's do that. If my memory serves me well, the two issues that arose yesterday were the length of cross-examination and an extra session or extra sitting to cover up time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct, though I think that the one that is already been resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's resolved by circumstances --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- but then it can be looked into in the next week. As to the question of the length of cross-examination, I don't think there is any order to be made here. The order is there, the guidelines are there. It's just a question of making sure that we implement them strictly. Now, in order to do that, is it possible to get an idea what time this witness began his evidence yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yeah, it was at 6.30, so I spent a little bit less than 30 minutes with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 6.30 on the 30th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So sorry. So at the end of the examination-in-chief, we will have to check how long it took you and then warn the Defence about the time. And the Chamber does intend to implement that guideline strictly henceforth. Any others thing to raise on that point? Mr. Milovancevic, do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. At least we've got it on the record. The next issue was the question of extra sittings to try and cover up on time. I could not agree more that we do need to cover up on that time. I am aware that it was discovered that in fact there are -- there is no time available, court time available, on Friday for an extra session. But looking at next week's courtroom schedule, it looks like Courtroom III is available on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday, and would there be any problem with us sitting the whole day on those -- any one of those three days?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- the suggestion for the extra sitting was -- came from the Prosecution, and it was really because we were very squeezed for this week. So it was kind -- it was really as a kind of measure to address this week, and I was thinking really just of one day. The difficulty -- I think there may be some difficulties in sitting full days for a number of days that are -- I think it does put quite a burden on witnesses who have to testify for that long a period of time. And I think also Defence counsel has indicated a number of difficulties that it poses both for him in terms of his preparation and also for the accused in terms of his health. So I certainly would not press that we sit extra days next week, but, of course, if the Trial Chamber decides that that is required, we'll do our best to accommodate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate what you do say. The pressure from the side of the Trial Chamber is to ensure that the Prosecution's case is completed as close as possible to the originally planned date. We already see that we are going to be out by four weeks. And we are trying to reduce that four-week period to -- if to zero, to zero; if not, to whatever we can do. So it is not just -- from the Chamber's point of view it's not just a question of this week. So having said that, the Chamber would appreciate, even if it is not sitting two sessions every day for three days but as we go along, an extra session somewhere if we can find one would be appreciated, just so that we cover up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. Just so the Court is aware, we still are aiming to finish by June 16th, though it may slip by a couple of days. But I would think even if we did not sit any extra days, I don't think it would slip by more than a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But originally you were finished by the 2nd of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right, of course. That was before the two-week -- the two weeks off that we had because of the health.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those are the two weeks I want to try and cover up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. And -- I think even if we sit an extra sitting, we are not going to finish substantially earlier than June 16. It's just -- just logistically becomes difficult to bring witnesses and get them scheduled and so forth. So I'm happy to sit an extra session as long as we know -- as long as we know in advance when it's -- you know, a number of days in advance when it's going to be. We can do our best to accommodate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you being the dominus litis, you would have to guide the Chamber because you would know when you're going to have your witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, we are constantly adjusting our schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So any time next week, if we sat an extra morning, that would be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's all I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At least because you are in the driving seat, you'll let us know if there is any need and we can try and schedule that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. I will say one thing, Your Honour, and I don't know if it -- if it -- I don't know if this will be of any assistance. But I'm not sure -- of course, the motion with respect to Milan Babic's evidence is pending. We understand that. I don't know what the contemplated schedule is for a decision from the Trial Chamber. I do think it will be impossible for us to rest our case without a decision on that motion. And I don't know if that poses any difficulty but I thought it's something I should raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't think it does. I think you will get your decision before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. I guess we can call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. I just had one other issue to raise. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So sorry. Mr. Milovancevic, you stand up -- you carry on Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Whiting has been standing quite often this afternoon; you can get a chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. As regards the additional sitting hours, it is the position of the Defence that this trial has been on for every working day for the whole week, full time, and we believe that the trial is following a normal procedure. The accused is of the same opinion. He was waiting for four years for the trial to commence, and in that sense, any proposal for additional hours depends on the assessment of my learned friends as to when their case could be finished. Their assessment was just an assessment, and if that is the only reason for additional hours, the Defence does not consider this any valid argument; however, that is one issue. But the second issue that is of essence for the position of the Defence is the fact that this trial calls for certain exertion on the part of all the participants. Every day after the sitting we have to prepare for the following day. If we have to sit a whole day, the work of the Defence counsel will be rendered more complicated and this additional effort under the circumstances, in our view, is absolutely not called for. It is not justified and it wouldn't be good. I agree with my learned friend that it would mean very little in the sense of gaining time or gaining momentum under the circumstances, as have been presented by Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. As there is no imminent sitting that is being discussed, I think we can let the matter rest at that point. We will re-look at it, as and when the needs arises. Yes, Mr. Whiting, you wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As Your Honour will recall, last week on the 26th of May the Trial Chamber ordered the parties to take certain steps with respect to three exhibits, three books that are in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Exhibits 24, 238, and 476. Now, two of those exhibits, two of those books, we are responsible for, the Prosecution, that's 24 and 476. With respect to those books, they are available - both complete B/C/S and English translations of the books - and we will have no difficulty making the selections and following the -- abiding by the Court's order by the date of the 2nd of June. With respect to the third book, however, the book that was put into evidence by the Defence, number 238, for that book there is only the B/C/S, and there is a very -- there are very brief selections which are translated into English, but there is not available an English translation. So that has slowed our review of that book, because it's obviously -- because it's not in English. So we have to have somebody, who understands the language and understands the issues, review the book to help us select the portion that we would like to put into evidence. So all I'm asking is if we could have an extra week to do -- with respect to that book, to accomplish the exercise that was ordered by the Court. So that if we could have that accomplished by June 9th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Given that that book was tendered by the Defence, is the Defence not able to provide a quicker translation of that? I would imagine the Defence would be in a position to meet the deadline of the 2nd of June, and couldn't they share that information with the Prosecution? Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as regards this book, the Defence at the moment when it started using it in these proceedings, wanted to have it all translated. However, it is a long book and the CLSS have asked us to mark only those parts that we were to use. It would take some time for the whole book to be translated, and we will ask the CLSS to do that. In the meantime, we will mark only those parts that we will be using. In any case, we believe that the 2nd of June deadline is far too short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You remember that the decision that was rendered last week indicated that only those relevant parts that the tendering party regards as relevant should be tendered. Therefore, the request is not that the entire book be translated but that the relevant parts be translated, Mr. Milovancevic. I can understand the position of the Prosecution wanting to understand the entire book so that they, themselves, can choose what they want to choose from the pages of the book as relevant. But from the point of view of you, who are tendering the document, all you need to do is to tender what you regard as relevant, not the entire book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. We have already marked those sections, and in that sense there shouldn't be any problem. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. In that event, then, you'll be held to the deadline of the 2nd of June, Mr. Milovancevic, and -- with respect to that book; and the Prosecution will be held to the deadline of the 2nd of June with respect to Exhibit 24 and 476 and the 9th of June with respect to Exhibit 238.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome. Next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness enters the court, yesterday I used -- I utilised a map which was marked by the witness, it was 65 ter 929. It was a map which depicted the Sector North. And as we finished at 7.00, I didn't manage officially to move this exhibit into evidence, so I would like to do it now and ask for the map, 65 ter 929 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May 65 ter 929 please be admitted into evidence and be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 745, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kirudja. I see you're surprised to see a completely different composition of the Bench. May the Court remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you took yesterday to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is okay. And thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kirudja. Ms. Richterova, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kirudja. Before we adjourned yesterday, we talked very briefly about people who you met after you arrived to the Sector North. You mentioned Lieutenant-General Nikovic, then you mentioned Slobodan Lazarevic. At this early stage, did you meet or did you pay any visit to any mayor in the Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this early stage, when we are talking about April 1992, we had to get going with the process of demobilisation and we began meetings from various places. The first instant where we met a mayor was just a week or so after my arrival in Sector North, when also the sector, the force commander, General Nambiar, also paid a visit. We had a large meeting in Petrinja, where the mayors and the commanders met us for the first time. This is about probably April 19 or something like that. Thereafter, we, of course, proceeded to continue our initial phase of the mission, meeting with the military commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: At this early stage, did you mean -- did you meet by any chance the mayor of Vrginmost?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this very -- this very early stage, Vrginmost was not particularly at the forefront. If you look at the map it's right inside, with -- not very close to the borders. Yes, we met him briefly but -- in the context of the military, we had a huge meeting in the hotel in Topusko, and he was there among other members, at this early stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During the time when you were working to implement the Vance Plan, were you able to observe how the Croatian side and the side of Croatian Serbs viewed the plan? Were there -- how did they interpret the plan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Even at this very early stage, our job was to interact, engage, both sides, meaning the signatories to the Vance Plan, the authorities in Zagreb represented on the other side of the confrontation line, and the other signatory of the Vance Plan was Belgrade authorities. But we weren't dealing with the Belgrade authorities in the sector, we were dealing with the Serbs who were inside the sector. Yes, we interacted with both, and again, at the early stages, the preponderance of meetings with the military on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And when you met them, did they -- these two sides, did they have the same opinions or did they -- opinions or the views of the plan, were they same or different?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time we noticed that they had different views, we had met in Sisak. We went to Sisak to begin to talk to them about where the confrontation line should be marked. We met with the Croatian side, at that time led by General Budimir, and we suddenly realised that they had a set of maps showing where the boundary that I showed you yesterday should be, their own map. We had our own maps, and when they saw our map, they said, "Wait a minute. We have a different map. Your boundaries is all wrong," they said. "Let's talk about this." And then we realised that they were interpreting the Vance Plan as follows: The boundaries of where the sector boundaries should be would be the outer edges of the civic borders of each of the named opstinas. I repeat, each of the named opstinas has a civic boundaries, and the outer boundaries of these opstinas would be the edge of our sector, UNPA. That's the Croatian interpretation of it. The facts on the ground were totally different. The Serbs had taken this war up to where they wanted to take it and defined a confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you at this very moment?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I have a map with me, and maybe it would be easier when you are explaining this situation to show it exactly on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It is -- it doesn't have a 65 ter exhibit number but it has ERN number which is 0400-7970. As yesterday, this is a big map, it's A3 format, so it would be difficult to display it on the screen. So I would like to provide the parties with map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While the map is being distributed, and for my sake, Mr. Kirudja, what's an opstina? Is it a village or a town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry about using that word. It is a Serbo-Croatian word that loosely stands for a municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If we could place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Is this on the e-court also?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It is on the e-court. If we could make it a little bit smaller? No, the other way around. Exactly. Perfect.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So if you could explain to us what you said, the edges of municipalities or opstinas, as you were using, and then the line where the Serbs -- the line where -- which Serbs reached.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for the helpful map. On this map, you can see that inside there is a blue colour and that on the blue colour, as you can see where I'm pointing at, what I called the edge, the civic boundary, at -- the edge of the opstina - in this case we are talking about Kostajnica - you see that the edge of the civic boundary goes this way, what I'm tracing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you are referring to the northern boundary on the map?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Northern boundary, the edge of the opstina named in the Vance Plan as Kostajnica. Its civic boundary would follow that course that I'm tracing now. When we come here, we switch from Kostajnica and then we get to Petrinja, and this course -- not Petrinja, no -- oh, no, I'm still in Kostajnica. And it goes that way, that way. And when we come in Petrinja, we pick up the northern edge of Petrinja and we continue this way. And when we come here, we pick up the northern edge of Vrginmost, and you continue this way - and this is still Vrginmost. And from here on we pick up the edges, the western edge, of Vojnic, and we continue this way. And we pick up the western edges of Slunj, and we continue down this way to -- as you can see. Now, there is a line that you will see, a thick line, this line.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Are you referring to line which is in red?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This line is actually where the confrontation line was. Was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That shows the actual situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. At that point, this is the map -- the map that we had drawn only had shown this confrontation line. Now, you can see there is now a difference between where the confrontation line is and where the edges of the civic boundaries of the opstinas are. At that time, when we were talking to the Croatian side in Sisak, our maps, and theirs, showed the difference between those areas, this area, you see that difference, you see this difference, in pink. They were shown in the maps in pink. You can see they are also shown here, this whole area from Slunj, see here. This whole area. And there is a confrontation line there. That difference became a major problem at the very beginning of the mission in the interpretation of how this -- both sides saw our role and it became a matter of Security Council resolution that said these pink zones have to be treated differently from the Vance Plan mandate that applies in the plan -- in the blue area. Now, to complete my explanation to you -- so I did seek to understand from the people who waged this war why they stopped where they stopped along that confrontation line. I had an evening discussion with General Spiro Nikovic, and he told me -- since he was the Yugoslav National Army commander for the 10th Corps, that covered the entire Sector North and parts of this, "Why did you stop there? Why did you put that confrontation line? And he said, "You see, we could take, as the Yugoslav National Army, this war beyond that confrontation line, but it wouldn't have served our purposes because the area beyond that confrontation line is predominantly peopled by Croats," especially the city of Karlovac which you see here, it's a major city, very close to the confrontation line. And Sisak, which you see here, is very close; and so is Zagreb, by the way, but you don't see it here in the map, or do you? You don't. He said, "We wanted this boundary to correspond to a natural boundary of where we want to take this conflict," and this boundary loosely corresponds to rivers Mrezinica, Kupa River, and on this side River Korana. They wanted a natural boundary.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to tender this map into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the map be given an exhibit number, and it is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it will be Exhibit 746, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You stated that this area was supposed to be treated in a different way. What do you refer to? Which way?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you recall yesterday, I said that our mandate as defined in the Vance Plan required all forces, armed, former Yugoslav National Army, to be totally demobilised, their weapons kept in storage, and the only permissible armed force were Milicija, what we call police, with only light side-arms. So in that case, the areas named in the Vance Plan would be devoid of all armed personnel other than ordinary police, what they call Milicija. And everybody had to pull out from that area, meaning the Yugoslav National Army and the Croatian army, which were close across the confrontation line. But when those areas of difference cropped up, the question was: What do you do or what is your mandate inside those areas that came to be known, in the correspondence you will see, as pink zones and were a subject of the Security Council resolution? The answer was: There, in those areas that are pink zones, not only would all parties pull out, but Croatian authority was to be restored sooner in those areas than the overall political settlement that I discussed yesterday that was yet to be found as to the disposition of the UNPA, United Nations Protected Areas. So the Croatian authority was supposed to be restored in those pink zones as quickly as possible, and also, the withdrawal of all the Serb elements in that pink area was also to be accomplished. That was the slight different treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And when you say "all Serb elements," do you also refer to police?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not only the military, but the police in the pink zones. The Serb police were not to operate in the pink zones either. It didn't turn out that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You already mentioned that the primary goal was to disarmament of JNA. Were you dealing -- did you participate in these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Full and for the 1st of April through May, yes, and that took us on whatever the commanders were on both sides, the Croatian controlled side and the Serb-controlled side and the Bihac pocket.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to now show you one of the row of reports. Did -- writing reports, was part of your duties?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is an essential part of our duty to prepare reports of every significant event and summarise -- and summarise our analysis of the situation as it developed. Usually they turned out to be weekly reports for -- civilian kind of reports coming from me, except where there was an incident that required immediate reporting and interpretation of what it meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What was the source of information which you put into your reports? Was it only what you personally observed or did you -- did you receive some information from other sources?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I explained to you, I was a full participant in all the meetings where the parties were involved in trying to implement the Vance Plan. I was also the reporting officer for the civilians who worked under me, and they would also submit and discuss with me the information they gathered. Thirdly, the military and the police also prepared reports which were also -- theirs were daily, I mean military and police, which were also available to me. So my reports embodied all these sources of information that would come to me in the course of the day, as I meet them, as I interact with them, and at the end of the day or the end of the week, I ask myself: What does all this mean in terms of our success or lack thereof in our mandated activities?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness 65 ter Exhibit Number 814. Can we scroll a little bit down? Can -- a message as in attached there --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three-page memo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Three-page memo. "Regards, C. Kirudja." Is it something that you prepared?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we go to page 2?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The date here is 30th of April and the subject is: "Meeting with General S. Nikovic." Do you remember this meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On 30th April, this must be one of the very earliest meetings that we held with Lieutenant-General Spiro Nikovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we scroll down a bit, a bit, a bit?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I want you to have a look at the third paragraph. Can you read it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which is it? The one that starts with the "General Nikovic ..." or the one starting with "One of the options ..."?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: "One of the options in consideration ..." And can you tell us the substance of what you were talking about during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an essential part of what I said that the JNA that was running and waged this war was to demobilise and hand over the weapons to us, and have all the personnel who were military lay down their arms. But as we started in this process, the announcement that there is a new reality shaping up in the former Yugoslavia by the general, saying that there will be the necessity for the officers who were conducting or who were in command of the established Yugoslav National Army, those who were not born in the area he called Serbian Krajina, had to relinquish their command earlier than others and get out, both this Serbian Krajina, and return to whatever it is that they were born. Remember, at that time the Yugoslavia before the war was one entity and the military commanders were coming from all over former Yugoslavia. When they were to hand over command of this area, which yesterday I mentioned that fell in three commands, those commanders who were there and were not born in that region will have to leave the area. And he -- at this time they were also concerned - at least the general was - what the state of relationship between the opposing forces, the Croat forces, would be like after he has demobilised. And that is the reference to: "They would have to leave certain weapons to counterbalance Croats who were now strengthening their positions," as you can see there between quotes. It was a concern they had. So this is what the paragraph generally was referring. There is more to it, but that's generally what the paragraph was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And if you could read for us the very last sentence in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Milicija and other armed units formerly under the JNA control will switch to the control of the Republic of Serbian Krajina or Bosnia-Herzegovina as appropriate."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It is what you already mentioned: Those who were born in Krajina would stay in Krajina, who were born in Bosnia would go to Bosnia or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is -- I must mention there is an another paragraph, I don't know whether it's covered at the top there, which puts that statement in context. He had begun by mentioning to us, and I quote: "There is a new reality in the former Yugoslavia. As of today," he said that day, "there will be six new republics formed out of the former Yugoslavia," and he proceeded to name them according to the way they should be. And you will see in the naming of those republics, he named Slovenia; Croatia; Bosnia and Herzegovina, as one entity; a new Yugoslavia formed by combining Serbia and Montenegro; and sixth Serbian Krajina as a new republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What was your reaction when he said there would be this sixth republic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we took note of it, but also it is obvious we knew that a concept of a Serbian Republic -- Serbian Krajina republic was inconsistent with the Vance Plan, and we knew that would be a problem because there was not to be an overarching authority, other than each of the opstinas running independently -- not totally independent but in a coordinated manner. So when that announcement was made it two elements of trouble. One, it would be an entity, and that other point that there would be weapons left behind to -- as you can see, already served notice that we have a bit of a problem here because we expect all weapons to be demobilised.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you -- did you make any comment to his announcement about -- that one of these countries will be also Krajina?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the first time we heard it. Normally when we hear something new, we don't debate about it, we just take note about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to go to the last page, which is page 4. It's -- in this paragraph, it says: "The recent emergence of a newly fortified Milicija is not hard to notice. Former military vehicles have been re-painted from green to blue, the colours of the present police force..." And it continues: "The JNA said seems to be taking advantage of the Vance Plan, which apparently excludes police units from those that must be demobilised, and their weapons put in storage." Is -- does it reflect this last paragraph -- does it reflect the reality in the field?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- it does, and at the very beginning of it -- because we were serving notice that there is a loop-hole in the Vance Plan that even at that early stage was being exploited and to prevent the intent and purpose of the Vance Plan, to have no armed elements in the UNPA. And we are serving notice that's what was happening even at that early stage. They had even begun, as you see earlier in the same report, talking about Territorial Defence forces for fear that if they totally were without these means of self defence, they were apprehensive even from that very early stage. When I say "they," I'm meaning the Serbs. That the Croats would take advantage because the Croats were not being disarmed by the Vance Plan, and that -- that loop-hole began to be their way to counterbalance that perception that they wouldn't be protected.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So did you see that -- what did you see in -- regarding to this last paragraph when: "Many of the Milicija men have begun to sport new blue uniforms," et cetera? Were you able to see this change?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because that is what we are observing. These are the people whom we are meeting from day to day, and one day you're wearing the military fatigue in green and then the next day you come in blue, so we noticed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me get that very clear. The people that you saw wearing these new blue uniforms were the same people who had been wearing the green JNA uniforms previously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some, not all of them. Some. And some who were in civilian clothes also were switched to blue uniforms. Like some mayors who the day before were wearing civilian clothes will come in blue uniform, some mayors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And did any of those people who were members of the police force, the Milicija, suddenly switch over to blue uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not suddenly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, did they --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gradually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did some of them also begin to wear blue uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they began to do that and actually also travel in vehicles which had been repainted from the green.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To blue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To blue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you meet with Nikovic after this initial meeting and discuss the withdrawal of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A number of meetings culminating to sometime in May when he presented a full plan of how the JNA were to withdraw. In between 30th of April and 25th of May there were plenty of meetings with General Nikovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did he also provide you with a list of all units which were in the area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I got a list of about a dozen or so units that were deployed. When I say "I," I mean military -- our military component. They are all colleagues to me. When the list is provided, it's also passed to me pass a civilian. It was a list of all the units that were part of the Banija command or Kordun or Lika that were in Sector North. As I remember, they were all at the brigade level and there were about a dozen of these units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I continue with another document, I would like to tender this document, 814, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document marked 814 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit Number 747, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness 65 ter exhibit number -- document 924.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you have a look at this document and tell us whether this list corresponds?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This bears a certain -- I recognise these brigade units. As I said most of them and if you -- probably there are about 12 of them or something like that, I don't see the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Is this the list --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Is this a list which you prepared based on the list which Nikovic provided you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a list that we worked with. I don't remember me personally working on it, but maybe a Chief of Staff or a military person preparing and handing it to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And at the bottom, if we could scroll down, also we can see weapons left behind by JNA?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What happened to these documents -- to these weapons?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the idea was according to the Vance plan, these units that had fought within this contested area would demobilise. The weapons that are listed there - and that were left behind by the Yugoslav National Army, as I mentioned earlier in one of the documents - these weapons were left behind for -- were to be in custody of the UNPROFOR in a double-key system - one key with a command, the Serb command, and the other key with UNPROFOR - and they will be in a storage guarded and controlled by UNPROFOR. That storage, what was in storage, comprised the weapons listed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were -- you also mentioned that some weapons were left behind as counterbalance for the possible attack. Did really some weapons stayed with, as you mentioned, with police or this Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And if you permit me a few minutes, the situation began to develop very fast. While we were trying, and to some extent succeeded, in putting these weapons under storage as per Vance Plan, on the ground, something else was happening. The Territorial Defence forces and the police were also taking positions along what they called borders of the RSK. And that was explained by their sense that the Croats would still attack them. Therefore, they began this process of deploying these -- first they were in blue but carried the weapons prohibited by Vance Plan because the Vance Plan permitted police only to carry side-arms. No, they had full-scale assault weapons, and they were deployed along the so-called RSK-bound border. And over time, they switched back to green, those which were deployed along that border, starting in the area of Slunj and ending the area of Petrinja, a whole cadre of force developed, deployed along the border.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when they switched from these blue -- from these blue uniforms into -- back to green?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would only give you a time-line, but we managed to get the weapons that you see on this screen put in storage around May, 25th of May and towards the end of May. Thereafter, what I described began to happen, and by two or three months, in August, there was a full-fledged unit more powerful than the police, that start to operate from the area of Slunj, commanded by one Colonel Novakovic and another one -- group centred around -- that group was centred in the Kordun area and another group centred in Banija under Colonel Tarbuk, and they were full-fledged military in green by the -- August or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I get some clarification? According to the Vance Plan, they were supposed to be demobilised and disarmed. You took these weapons and you put them in storage. The weapons that were left for counterbalancing were left with who? With the Milicija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's obvious that we didn't take all the weapons; that's the implication in storage. That actually they did get weapons. Now, where they were coming from, Your Honour, I can't tell you where but it's not difficult to imagine. I remember yesterday I also showed you the boundary between the UNPA, where it was completely nominal, between the UNPA and other areas of Bosnia. So they could travel freely and Bosnia was fully armed. So the Serbs were on that part from Kostajnica through Dvor. The boundary within the sector and in Bosnia was only nominal because they controlled both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. But you say it's obvious you did not get all the arms back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Either we didn't get all of them or new ones came in through any number of ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, when you say they were -- these weapons were kept under lock and key --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Double key.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Double lock and key, what do you mean by "double"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the Vance Plan envisaged that there would be a continuance of hostility on both sides, the mission itself was not even charged with the responsibility of politically trying to solve the issue; that was left somewhere else, in the ICFY. The designers of that peace agreement allowed that there could be a reason for it by implication, because they said, You put them in storage, one key -- like a bank, when you go into a bank to get your private -- the bank comes with one key and you come with another key. Similar thing. If you ever wanted to take those weapons for whatever reason - though we didn't even envisage they would be taken - you have a key with UNPROFOR and a key with the Serbian command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My last question before I hand you over back to Ms. Richterova. To your knowledge, were any weapons removed from storage without the knowledge and consent of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not in that sense, but at a certain time, war broke out and they came in and took the weapons, and four times we had a war breaking out. We'll get into that if the counsel get you there. They were taken out for the purposes of waging a war later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In fact, we can jump ahead of [sic] time, and when you said that these weapons were taken, were they taken by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are the ones with the second key.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. And when was it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, towards the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what was the purpose?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a war that followed, because the Croats took some precipitous actions, beginning very far away from Sector North in a place called Maslenica; and remember, these sectors spread all over. We are only talking about Sector North. An action taking place in Sector South or Sector East or Sector West would precipitate a reaction from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So these -- were these weapons taken before the Croats attacked Mas --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, after.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It was after?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they were taken again when there was an attack in Medak pocket.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Does it mean that there were still some weapons left?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the storage?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, after they took them out, the first time, they never put them back all over again, it would be -- no. We never returned to the status quo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you. We were talking about this meeting with Nikovic who provided you with the names of the brigades and units which were deployed in the area. Did he say when and under which conditions which would JNA with -- would withdraw from this area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Spiro Nikovic was a very, very correct military officer, one I still remained admiring in trying to do a difficult job. Actually, he intended to accomplish what the Vance Plan did and did run into trouble. As a matter of fact, he didn't even complete his tour because about a week or so after this, he called us again to Bihac and let out a bomb-shell and said: I'm now a retired general. He had been relieved of his command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So when you say "after a week," are you referring to this meeting on 29 of April?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He had been even for -- for his own expectation he was surprised, but as a soldier, he didn't -- didn't mince words. He just said: I'm -- from now been -- I'm a retired general. Now, going back to your question, he had tried, against some opposition, to accomplish this demobilisation. And I say "some opposition" because a lot of officers below him, particularly even if the sector, opposed what he was doing, the demobilisation. But he accomplished it any way, and he did order -- as a general -- the ranking -- the most-ranking general, he did order them to proceed as required, notwithstanding the opposition. So on that day, on 29th, when he had been relieved of his command, within a day, I got word from Lazarevic, probably in Kordun, telling me: Go tell him that he's no longer welcome here, and if he sets foot in this place we shall arrest him. And I knew that warning was not a vague one then, so I did take a car and drove at night. By 8.00 I got into Bihac to warn him that this is now the situation: You're no longer in command and you have this warning, take heed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me understand you. General Nikovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- heard for the first time from you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- that he's relieved of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. He's the one who told us that he is relieved --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- of his command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As soon as the word got out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, he was the one that the unit in the sector reported to as the ranking general. The moment that word got out, that got to me, that: Tell him now, he's no longer welcome here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Before we continue I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence, may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 748, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to ask you something which we started talking about already yesterday. You mentioned that there were three command zones, one in Kordun, the other one in Banija, and the third one in Lika, which in fact was not in Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was partly in Sector North.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Before this -- before the JNA withdrew, did General Nikovic talk to you about the involvement -- did he talk about involvement of Belgrade with this withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and in very clear terms. He even mentioned a legal fact, said that this peace agreement is signed in Belgrade and in Zagreb, and this was in reference to the resistance he was encountering about getting his order about demobilisation. He said: What is decided in Belgrade for us is orders for us, and this is what should be done. Belgrade had decided at that moment all officers in that area who were not born there must leave; that had only consequences immediately in Banija and for himself. He was from Montenegro. And the commander of Banija at that time, General Rakovic, was also from Montenegro. So those were affected by those orders almost immediately, and somebody else had to take command. Not so in Kordun because the commander was Cedo Bulat and Cedo Bulat comes from Vrginmost.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In this respect, I would like to ask you, did he mention how many -- how many, let's say, Serb soldiers would go to Bosnia, in percentage, and how many would stay in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recall some percentage, but I don't have it in my mind right now, I need some refreshment. But he did mention something like that. I'm not clear right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did he mention whether it would be significantly small amount of soldiers who would stay in, for example, in Bosnia or, on the other hand, significantly big number?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not talking about soldiers, counsel. He was talking about the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Commanders.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the commanders, obviously, are not that many -- actually he did mention that the order affected -- there would be about 13 commanders left in there. The rest of them have to go back to Serbia or wherever they came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, I want to go back to these three operational or command zones, Kordun, Banija, and Lika. What happened after the JNA withdrew? What happened to these command zones?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Interesting that not much changed. They remained pretty much the way the JNA had organised them, except for the change of command. The greatest change was in Banija, where, as I said, there was a ranking general there, who when Spiro Agnew -- Spiro Agnew, I'm sorry, an American name. Spiro Nikovic had been relieved of his command, Rakovic took over temporarily. And he himself having come from Montenegro was also relieved of that command, and eventually the command in Banija settled around Colonel Tarbuk, towards the end. There were others in between, but since they were changing so fast. Suffice it to say that command settled by the longest time I was there around Colonel Tarbuk. In Kordun, it didn't change because Cedo Bulat fitted the criteria. He didn't have to leave. He was in command before. He remained in command. In Lika, that didn't -- I didn't follow that in great details because most of their command was in Sector South, and only a small part of their command was in Sector North. I'm talking about that area known as Plaski, that fell under their command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And can you judge whether the command structure was significantly smaller or bigger or the same after the -- after the withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Remained the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And gradually, this command operational zones and the soldiers gradually, how were they referred to?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Referred to? It started in that meeting that you referred to on the first slide, when we were getting the weapons and the units, they were at that time only referred to as Territorial Defence forces, TDF, in our documents. And within a short time - "short time" meaning months - they had developed into an army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I think it is a time for adjournment or a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Richterova. We are going to take a short break and we will come back at 4.00. Thank you very much. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, you mentioned that according to the Vance Plan, there shouldn't be any overarching government beyond each of the opstinas, some kind of umbrella government. Did you learn that such a government really exist in this area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it came very early, again, in the -- in April, where the same man I referred to earlier, Slobodan Lazarevic, came and announced that we now -- very, very happy, very gleefully, we now have our own government. And I said, Where? And he said, It's in Knin. And I said, What's the name? Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you try to meet with some representatives of this government?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One, there was no need for me to do so under the terms of my job. Everything that I was required to do was in Sector North. If the government was in Knin, that was somebody else's responsibility. My counterpart there was Victor Andreev, so that was not my immediately of my concern. What was of my concern immediately was after he announced that there was a government of Serbian Krajina, he also began to do certain things that were in all effect an interference with our job and the local staff that we hired.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you give us very briefly some examples?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first thing was because they were government of Serbian Krajina, they wanted us, as the United Nations, to consult with them for those of the local people that we hire, something we were not prepared to do, nor do we do then or now. Wherever the UN is deployed, whoever we hire is our business. And the second element of interference was when he began, and some of their police, to request to see passports of different personnel in the -- who were with the UN. That interference continued to the extent at one time I was already outside the sector in a meeting of a military nature, when I came back to find out he had organised the forceful removal of one of our interpreters whom we had hired locally by the name Indira Kulenovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: May I interrupt you here?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness 65 ter Exhibit 816.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While the exhibit is coming on the screen, did you employ a large number of local people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, large is relative, in the sense that this was not a very large mission. We had a substantive number of people, like interpreters, there were contractors to do certain things, but not very large compared with other missions that I have known, too -- I have known, where we have a much larger component.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you please scroll it down?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Is this one of the memos prepared by you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I recognise that too is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we go to page 2?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This document is dated 15 of May 1992, and it is meeting with the president of parliament, Republic of Serbian Krajina. You stated in this document that present were Mr. Mile Paspalj, president of the parliament of the Republic of Serbian Krajina; and you also mentioned Mr. Toso Paic, Deputy Minister of the Interior and commissioner of police for Kordun. Can we stop here for little bit, and can you tell me how did you learn or why did you use this term, "Deputy Minister of Interior"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of this memo or earlier? Because there is the context of the memo, the circumstances being addressed in this memo, and if I understand your question earlier about the title of Toso Paic, it didn't arise from the context of this memo but I can still tell you how it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Please, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Earlier on, and I briefly mentioned yesterday, that the same Lazarevic had come to my office earlier than the incident being addressed by this memo, to tell me that if I wanted to have anything that involved the police, the most important person I should know about was Toso Paic. And he told me, one, he had the title of commissioner of police for Kordun but he was also Deputy Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did he, Lazarevic or anybody else, did he also tell you what was his relationship, working relationship -- I will rephrase it. Who was his superior?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If he was the deputy, I asked, Who is the Minister of Interior? That's natural to ask. And he told me, Mr. Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did he tell you anything about the relationship between a minister and deputy minister?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point, please recall that I'm being told something which I interpreted to be inconsistent with my -- our mandate, there is an overarching authority. I am not also at liberty to encourage that. So other than getting bare minimum of the information I needed, I didn't at that time want to go into the great details, who was the minister, when were they appointed, because it's already a problem that there is an overarching issue. So I got all the minimum information that I needed in the earliest incidents, and I repeat when he told me this, he didn't even present Mr. Paic. He just mentioned the name, Mr. Paic. It took days before I would actually meet Mr. Paic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Going --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Before you proceed, could I hear from you what the acronym CCAO stands for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I actually referred to that yesterday when I said that at the earliest beginning I had been given that title, chief civil affairs officer, which was revised in months and stabilised for all sectors to CAC, which stood for civil affairs coordinator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And SC?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: SC stands for sector commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: SMPAO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: SMPO is senior military -- where does it appear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: In the -- in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It is in the first line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: With the SC where the CCAO --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And the other acronym that follows. S -- it looks to me like SMPAO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. That -- that one, I'm not even clear whether there's a misspelling because the only other person who must have been there would have been police officer. Therefore, that chief of CIVPOL, who probably had that -- it could mean a lot of things. It either mean the civil police or the military -- senior military police. There were also some military police around. So it was one of the two. And that -- I have to refer to it back again. It doesn't stand out to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which one is that now? Senior military police, which one is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also present with the SC were the CCO, meaning myself; the SMPO, the chief of CIVPOL; and UNPROFOR's local interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, but you didn't say what AMPO is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the one I'm having difficulty recollecting who it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In the second paragraph, you stated, "The meeting was convened as a matter of urgency following a series of actions by local police against UNPROFOR personnel," and it is what you --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's what I had begun to explain with the announcement that there had been established a Serbian Republic in Krajina where they began to insist that they should get all the employees locally vetted by them. And when we told them that was not acceptable, they proceeded anyways. And the first precipitous action that was taken along that line was the arrest of this local staff member. When I returned to Topusko, I recall that day I was out, she had been rounded up and arrested and held at Vrginmost police station. And when I came, I found out that that was the case, and I did take several actions as a result of that arrest of Ms. Kulenovic. One was to do something that put her into safety, and that is transferring her to -- out of the sector. But I also had to take issue with this action by the local authorities, which I considered not only not a welcome, but it was a violation of a number of things and an interference with the United Nations mandate. And not knowing now how the nexus of how this matter was created, it occurred me if they are telling me there is a government in Knin, who did I have in Sector North that would give me a way of addressing and talking about that? It occurred that I had learned that along with other positions that they had established as part of that government in Knin, there was the position of the president of Serbian Republic Assembly, what you would in other countries call the Speaker of the House, but he was called president of the Serbian Republic Assembly, Mile Paspalj. And I also had learned that Mile Paspalj, of course, was a resident of Sector North, specifically his place of residence was in Glina. I also realised that he was a particularly important personality because the actual agreement, the agreement that put into effect the Vance Plan, was signed on behalf of the Serbs by Mile Paspalj because the original person requested to sign, Milan Babic, didn't want to sign it. On that account, I realised that he waged a lot of importance, and I asked to see him so that I can protest this action because it's a violation of the mandate which he signed as representing the Serb side. So I quickly called that meeting, and the people shown in this memo were in attendance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And when you lodged the complaint, was it Paspalj who replied?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Interesting, I only wanted to see him and I got the appointment time. When I showed up in his -- in his -- where he worked out of in Glina, I was surprised who else turned up - and I hadn't even mentioned to him about my demarche, the one I wanted to make - it was Toso Paic. He had been invited obviously, by Mile Paspalj because he had asked what is the nature of my meeting. And I said, About this abuse of the authority and the -- the staff member. And when I started my complaint, kind of laid out, it was Toso Paic who responded. Mile Paspalj just stood there quietly and listened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were all these complaints at the end settled?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was important that -- I was actually quite happy that Mr. Paic had shown up because this was a police action, and the police action had been taken in Kordun specifically by the chief of police in Vrginmost, one Djuro Skaljac who had taken that action. The charge sheet that I was shown was also from Vrginmost. In short, Mr. Paspalj [sic], in his capacity, as he said - I was the commissioner of police for Kordun - this was a mistake, we didn't -- anyway, he did reverse the whole course they had taken by -- by saying, by conceding that it was not an action that his police would have wanted to take and it was a mistake, it was a misunderstanding, and it wouldn't happen again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what about the other issues which you mentioned, checking the passports --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That too, they began to justify that the reason why we were checking all this was because we didn't want you to wander around, you might be in trouble with the local people, you might run into mines, but sorry, we won't do that again either.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we -- can this document be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 749, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I just was informed that we have a small error in the transcript. Page 38, line 25, instead of "Mr. Paspalj," there should be "Mr. Toso Paic" because it says, "in his capacity, as he said ... the commissioner of police for Kordun." So it was just a small error. Can we now, please, display 65 ter Exhibit 817?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was -- is this another report prepared by you?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we scroll it down, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That, too, is my handwriting on the front of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we go to page number 2?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The date is 16 of May, 1992, and it's statement of the president of parliament, Republic of Serbian Krajina. Is this document a continuation of your reporting about the meeting with Mile Paspalj, or were there two separate meetings?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a continuation. When the incident had passed, the incident involving the interpreter had passed, Mile Paspalj actually began to seize on the opening that I had created by inviting him, to give us the benefit of his thoughts about how the mission was being carried out and the issues that he saw as important.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will ask you to make comment on two brief passages from your report. The first one is second paragraph, the first sentence, which reads, "The Republic of Serbian Krajina does not have an army, the people are the army, and when UNPROFOR talks about withdrawal, it should be understood that our people could not withdraw from here." And then I would want to refer you to fourth paragraph, the last two sentences, "We want to establish the state of Serbian Krajina," said the president, "in order to survive." He made reference to atrocities attributed to the other side during the Second World War and added that his people do not wish to be extinct. Can you make a comment on this? What did -- what did you discuss with Mile Paspalj about this establishment of state of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please scroll this document to the top where the date is visible? Thank you. You can see that date is in May, the middle of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While you're on the date, what does 1310, 14, stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the middle -- the third line of that first paragraph, it says, the meeting was at Glina on 1310, 14 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's military. It means it took place at 1.00 -- it's a military time. These documents were all reflecting the fact that we were largely a military establishment. The transmission of this document was being done by a military company, specifically a Dutch military communications unit. So all the reference to date and time were in military format.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Although this is ten past 1.00 on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you please continue if you want to --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The date is May. The incident is -- the content of the -- of the document is after that incident that we had talked -- we have just talked about. What was going on then, apart from the incident, was the demobilisation effort. At that time we were in full swing, asking for identification of all the units, all the forces, with a view to asking that they all be demobilised and the arms taken into storage. And Mile Paspalj, of course, knew about that what was going on on the military side. This was the beginning of a constant policy line, constant concern, that the people who were in these UNPA would not be properly protected by UNPROFOR because UNPROFOR didn't have all the force they thought was needed to ward off, to contain, a perceived threat to come from their opponent, namely the Croatian side of the conflict. Even if on the military side, remember this is the 16th of May, General Spiro Nikovic is still ordering and gathering all the weapons to be put in storage, I said earlier this morning there were people opposed to that effort. The logic of why they were opposed and what it is, he is now beginning to voice that logic, one, it is we don't even have arms for you to take into storage. It's a rhetorical statement because obviously we do and we have them. We can see them. They are on the streets. They are in the form of tanks, artillery, APCs. Secondly, most of the people, ordinary people, they all -- even when they are not particularly involved in any services, you'll find them carrying weapons. So what he was talking about was to prepare ground for their argument that they don't have to lay down their arms, and they were not in agreement that all these weapons be taken. And lastly, the last paragraph you mentioned, was we are in the process of creating a new state for ourselves, and, of course, all the elements of a state, other than boundaries, it's a government, and part of the government is an army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, during the time you were there, did you had frequent or infrequent contacts with the local Serb mayors in Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I alternatively would meet on the military side -- and because I had this other part of the mandate to be completed, we would also meet on the civilian side, and that civilian side meant either we are meeting with the mayors or we are meeting with the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When meeting these people, was there anything common about their views, their expressions, about what was their desire for the political structure under which they want to live?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it varied with each mayor, from those who were completely silent and did their jobs and were not giving any -- were not very vocal, if at all, on political views - and that would -- was best represented by the mayor of Vrginmost, the late Obradovic - to those who were very vocal about political issues and how they saw the future in Croatia, represented perhaps best by the mayor in Petrinja, who was very vocal. Those who were very vocal engaged us very early. As I recall from day one, when we met in Petrinja, this was on 19th of April, when I mentioned earlier that the General Nambiar had come to visit there, those speeches began in earnest and they went something like this. Mr. Kirudja, they will tell us -- and whoever it is they were addressing, We think you should understand one basic fact here. We have had this war because we can't live together as Serbs and Croats. The sooner -- I remembered the words. The sooner you understand that, the better for us, we can't live together as Serbs and Croats. And we would like to have our own area where we are, as Serbs, in control. That's the gist of those speeches.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What was your reaction? What was your response to this?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: None, because, as I have mentioned earlier, our mandate did not include any political settlement because that was left in the international conference for the former Yugoslavia where all the issues of political concerns were being addressed. Other than listening to that we wouldn't even engage in a debate about it because we would be getting outside our mandate. Our mandate did not include looking at the future vision or looking at how this land that was called the United Nations Protected Area, how it will finally be disposed of, so we didn't engage beyond listening.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that you had been told, We can't live together as Serbs and Croats, and we would like to have our own area where we are, as Serbs, in control. Did they also mention any connection with other Serbian areas in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not so directly other than in action and fact. They acted it out; they didn't have to say it. An example what I just said: I did obviously go to each headquarters of the mayors. The example what I'm saying is played out best in Dvor, when I went to Dvor to meet the mayor of Dvor. The mayor of Dvor at that time, Yugoslav Borojevic, was interested with other things than what I was going to talk about, the implementation of the Vance Plan. He was interested in getting us to get involved with the removal of some 10.000 people or so from across the border into Bosanski Novi, and he was in touch with the other side of -- his counterpart in Bosanski Novi, to the extent that he will tell me, I have the mayor of Bosanski Novi here, come to talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, I will interrupt you. I want to talk about this particular event.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: But before we move there, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
