utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 5 -- 750.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And before, before we start talking about the events in Bosnia, I would like to show you the last document from this area, which is 65 ter 819. Can you recognise this document? It is written by you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we go to page 2? This document is dated 18 of May, 1992, and it says, meeting at Glina, 1811 hours, May 1992. Present at the meeting, and among others, there were president of the district court of justice and district prosecutor for the courts in both Kordun and Banija. What was the primary purpose of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had called this meeting which took place in the town hall of Glina basically to begin to explain to the civilian authorities what it is we are doing, and to hear and gauge their understanding of the same. And because of the various aspects our mandate covered, we not only invited the mayor, we also invited those who were in charge of the system of justice.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we move to page 3? Can we scroll little bit down?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I want to refer to paragraph 2 on this page. Yes, it starts with, "The community leaders..." I will read for you couple of sentences, and if you could make a comment. "The community leaders went on to state that the EC, in particular, was trying to prejudge the political outcome of the conflict. The EC, they said, is attempting to give a special status to the RSK which, according to the local community, is contrary to the Vance Plan. It will not be possible, they added, to resolve the political problem without the legal representatives of this area and the RSK." Can you please comment on this paragraph or section of this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said earlier, one of the things I wanted was to gauge their understanding of what it is that we, as the UNPROFOR, were supposed to achieve in this area. And I mentioned yesterday the EC, the monitors from European Community, were on the ground, well before the deployment of UNPROFOR in this area. Again, this memorandum is on 18th of May. We are in the middle of accomplishing the demobilisation, or attempting to accomplish, the demobilisation. These being community leaders, this is Glina, this is the headquarters of Mile Paspalj, the other person who had spoken along the lines that we would like to establish our own Krajina for the purposes of achieving a number of objectives, among them their own security. In this particular paragraph, the message was being sent to me that they didn't agree or appreciate what they were hearing from the European Community. The European Community monitors, though they were not in the meeting, were also not very involved with us. They had their own separate and parallel mandate. In this particular paragraph, where they are referring to that the EC is attempting to give a special status to the RSK, which according to the local community is contrary to the Vance Plan, it's another way of saying they didn't -- the European Community was not in support of an overarching entity called RSK. And the European monitors would have been much more forthright in saying they don't support it. When the local people are saying that the European interpretation of what was happening in RSK is contrary to the Vance Plan, their interpretation itself was contrary to the Vance Plan. They were just using this opportunity to simply say, We don't like what they are doing here. We can't agree with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Last question about this document. Was there a prison in Glina?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a very sizeable prison in Glina, a very large one, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you have any dealings with local authorities regarding some prisoners in this prison?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I did actually take the opportunity to go and look into that prison because it did contain a number of people being held in there, not just from Sector North but from far beyond, some even from Sector West, others from Bihac pocket that were being held there. And in particular, because we were always responding to both sides of this conflict, the Croatians, they were constantly talking to us about Croats who were being held in prisons in there. So part of the reason we kept an eye to that prison and what was going on was to be able to respond to them that, yes, such and such prisoner is or isn't in that prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And were you also involved in release of some of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit 751, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Are you able to estimate how many people you facilitated the release of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, because this question, I answered in the full time. Because over the two years when I was there, there was a good number of people who were in and out at different times, so the number is not right in my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But are you at some stage able to give the overall number of the people over the period of two years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Based on one incident that took place or -- either in August or September, where a large number of Muslims were being held in Glina -- when I'm talking about large numbers, I'm talking about tens of them. I don't know, probably reached even almost to 100. And it had been an incident where an operation had been undertaken from the Muslim side on the Plaski area, a military operation, that attempted to cross Sector North. They were intercepted by the Serb border police, a couple of them were killed and a large number of them were taken prisoner, and they were taken to Glina. And we were involved in a lot of discussions about those prisoners. That group alone, later on they were released. It's a large group. There were individuals in between, so that's why the number is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But they were a military group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They had -- they had forced their way across.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to show document 65 ter 834.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And before this document is displayed, just going quickly back to the Judge's question. You mentioned a release of some Muslims. Who were primarily the people who you were involved -- you were involved in their release? Were they Serbs, Croats, or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not involved in the common criminals or those who fell in the category of common criminals in the streets of Glina or somewhere who were Serbs. We were only involved when the prisoners were either Croats or Muslims and their plight had a political dimension to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now we have on the screen another document. Can you recognise whether it was written by you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This one is not my handwritten. Usually that my staff will -- when I became very busy, they would transmit documents authored or released by me and since they had to go and take them physically to the Dutch transmitters, I authorised them this time they can put the cover which was necessary for transmission. This particular one was one of my staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is the name at the bottom there not your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my name but the handwriting is not my handwriting. I just -- you might have realised there is a difference between this handwriting and the previous document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we go to page 2?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This document is dated 8 of June, 1992. Was this memorandum then prepared by you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In first -- the subject is: "Investigative report on the displaced people observed in Bosanski Novi." In the first paragraph, you mention people observed as being held in a stadium at Bosanski Novi, and then paragraph 3 starts, "On 26 May, the CAS" -- I'm sorry, "CAC, met with the mayor of Dvor," et cetera, et cetera. Is this the meeting when you started talking about before I interrupted you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell very briefly what this meeting was about, what Mr. Borojevic wanted from you.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I began to say earlier, I wasn't really going there to talk about Bosanski Novi. Bosanski Novi is in Bosnia and Herzegovina; it was outside of our mandate. I was just going to the opstina of Dvor to talk about implementation of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can I stop you for a second? Can you tell us where Bosanski Novi is?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's across the River Drina, Drina or whatever, that river, there is a river across, and it is inside Bosnia and Herzegovina. At this moment, I believe it was renamed, I don't know what the new name it has now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We can see it in the concise atlas on page 21, grid C3.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And it is right on the border.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Across the river.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Across the river. And then it's -- it's River Una?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: River Una, sorry. Thank you. You could see -- if you were stationed at where the company, the Danish company was operated from Dvor, you can, if you have good eyesight or binoculars, you could see across to where the incident was taking place without physically even being there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So now you are referring to the --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the incidents in this memo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In the first paragraph about these people observed at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So can we go back to the meeting, what Mr. Borojevic wanted from you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. And I was beginning to illustrate where the cooperation between the Serb authorities in the UNPA and the Serb authorities across in Bosnia and Herzegovina was a given and went naturally; you didn't have to discuss it. It was happening on a day-to-day. So on this particular meeting, while we were coming to talk about the Vance Plan, the entire thing was changed by the mayor, because we wanted to talk about what was going on in Bosanski Novi. And I was taken aback by that request and he said, "We have a request," to me as the UN representative in this sector, from the mayor of Bosanski Novi. And I said to myself, But I don't have much to do with the mayor of Bosanski Novi. And he still proceeded to tell me about what he wanted. And when I declined to do so, he dialed the mayor on the telephone and he said, "The mayor is on the phone here. Please talk to him." Still, I politely told him that it has to be done at a different place and different time; in other words, whatever these groups were doing was almost seamless. If they are Serb on the Bosnian side and if they are Serb on the UNPA, it was total cooperation, it was seamless cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So he -- mayor of Dvor Na Uni asked you about to do something --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: -- in relation to people in Bosanski Novi. What was your reaction? What --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First is that of total surprise because, as summarised in this -- if you can scroll this document up, please. No, up. See that A, B, there, that was the gist of what he wanted to talk about, that we would participate -- he would request us, as the United Nations, to participate in a process that would have led to the transition of these people in Bosanski Novi through the sector and out into Croatia, and to guarantee that none of them remained in the sector and they were going to get out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because the first thing I wanted to know is what was this all about? Why are they moving? What is causing them to move? All that I needed to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did he mention -- I'm sorry, I probably missed it. Did he mention who were these people who wanted to leave, what nationality?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So did you receive -- did you receive the answer what made them to leave? Why did they wanted to leave?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This came -- there is a small sequence, I briefly will tell you. The first notification was from Mayor Borojevic, mayor of Dvor. He delivers the message that the mayor of Bosanski Novi, Mr. Pasic, wants to talk to you about this matter. I decline to talk about the matter. I returned to Topusko. Within a day or two, Mr. Pasic himself, not mayor of Dvor, shows up in my office, the mayor of Bosanski Novi, along with a group of people. And that's when we start -- I start getting answers to the questions you are asking: Who are these people? Why they want to move?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What was his answer when you asked him why?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first thing was a story that was difficult for me to appreciate because they were all Serbs and they were talking about Muslims voluntarily wanting to leave, and they underscored the word "voluntarily" want to leave their homes. And I said, you are the mayor is -- why would people voluntarily in those numbers, want to leave? What's going on? And it -- bottom line was, well, they were not really voluntarily trying to leave. They had a situation developing. And I said, What kind of situation? That's when I got the -- an answer, We also have a new Republic of -- Republic of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina, a new entity is announced. And these Muslims would not swear loyalty to this new entity. We told them that if they don't swear loyalty to this entity, they must leave. And I said, Then they are not leaving voluntarily. And so on the conversation, the bottom line, we established that they were being forced out, they were not leaving voluntarily, and they were -- and Mr. Pasic was asking us to participate in making refugees out of people from their own homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, at this time when you met Mr. Pasic for the first time, did you agree to participate at their departure to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not only I didn't agree. When they realised that I don't agree, he wanted to know who I reported to so that he can go and get over some -- the boss. And I told him, You can go all the way to the Secretary-General. This is not going to change. We don't make refugees out of people in their homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can I move this document into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit 752, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I want to show you 65 ter document 842. Can you recognise whether it is written by you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's written on my behalf.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And can we go to page 2? This document is dated 3rd of July and subject is: "Humanitarian aid." Do you remember whether you prepared this memorandum?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This document again in the first or, better say, the second paragraph is talking about the football field in Bosanski Novi. Can you very briefly say what in fact happened in this -- on this football field? Why it is always mentioned in this, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Note that this it's in July. The date of that is July, if you look at the top. The top of the document. That's in July. And if you recall, the earlier incident when we are talking about football field was in June, much earlier. The incidents about people gathering in the football field, quite briefly, this is what happened in June, not in July. The soldiers, the Danish soldiers, sitting in Dvor, observing with binoculars at that football field. On a clear day they just saw a good number of people on buses being shuttled into the field, into the field, and one of them was particularly observant that those people sat and formed an SOS, human SOS. And he realised that there was trouble, but we didn't know what trouble was because it was across, and in Bosnia. We told -- or I did, I told my headquarters about it. The military told in a different channel the same thing, and my colleague from UNHCR, I sent him because the mandate of UNHCR had more flexibility to go and get more information. We did all of that. Now, the memo you are showing here is a bit of an inside problem in the UN where the paragraph is a bit of a complaint by me that, I told you all this, you ignored it, now you want me to talk about it again when it has -- it has finished. That's what the paragraph is talking about, our frustration is not to investigate; it's the fact that we have already brought this matter to the headquarters' attention but it wasn't paid attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you subsequently learned who were the people at the -- in the football stadium?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was the beginning of this number of people in Bosanski Novi, particularly being rounded from a village called Blagaj, that they were sorting them out in the process that I mentioned briefly earlier, when they wouldn't swear allegiance to the new Republika Srpska. And this is the group that eventually was actually forcefully removed from Bosanski Novi through Sector North.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So we are referring to Muslims?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, again they were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to read you the second paragraph, of course, only portion of that second paragraph. "We believe the football field detainees are only a tip of the iceberg involving the concerted action of local Serbian authorities in BiH trying to establish a Serbian Republic of BiH free of Muslims. In that process, the mayors, the Milicija, and TDF of Bosanski Novi acting in unison with their counterparts, not only in the UNPA, Dvor and Kostajnica, but also with Bosanska Dubica, Banja Luka, Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc." When you mention "acting in unison," can you elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first notification from -- about this matter was delivered by the mayor of Dvor, a Serb based in Dvor. He didn't even say, I'm delivering a message; it was more or less like a common cause. They demanded a number of things which we have just discussed about transitioning through the sector and calling international media to watch that this was going on. And now the fact that the mayors of Bosanski Novi felt free -- just cross and come to my office with no notification and begin to discuss the same thing. No Muslims couldn't cross that border. Every time a Muslim crossed that border, we had to -- we had an issue because the Serbs wouldn't let them. Neither would Croats. Just the Serbs would cross that border without any problem, whether they are mayors or not mayors. Not only that it was the mayor of Bosanski Novi who came. Later on, in a second visit, after the first one, he brought the representatives of all these -- of all these towns, Bosanska Dubica, Sanski Most, and Kljuc, they were all in my office, both mayors and police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So does it mean that after you refused to participate, that this attempt to move these Muslims continue?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It continued and to my chagrin, they -- I'm condensing the story, it -- bottom line is that they got permission from UNHCR and the Croats that they can move the fast -- the first batch that they wanted to move, notwithstanding our strong objection to it, and I'm talking about a strong objection that I had sent to both my headquarters and to UNHCR headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can I move this document into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit 753, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to display 65 ter document 843.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This document is dated 6 of July, 1992, and it is Srpska Republika, Bosnia-Herzegovina, opstina Bosanski Novi Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We have on the screen B/C/S version. Is it possible to have English, please? Thank you. Can we slowly scroll it down?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait just a second. I still have B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, do you have English version or B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one that is in front of me?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the English one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm fine now. I've managed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document? Have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to go to third paragraph from the bottom. And it says, "In relation to citizens requesting and in order to provide them personal and property safety, we organise the meeting between representatives of Bosanski Novi municipality, Dvor, and above-mentioned Crisis Staff on date of 6 July, when if agreed on mutual satisfaction they is need organised departure," it's how it is stated, "with buses of companies, Kozara Prevoz, Autoprevoz, Dvor." And then the second paragraph from the bottom, "Safeguarding to the convoy they will be provided," here it's provide, "by internal affairs of Republic of is Serbian Krajina workers." What, in gist, what this document is talking about, is it the agreement of -- for the departure of these people or what is it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was one of those bases why I used the word "unison," acting in unison, concerted effort of the Serbians in both sides. If you look at the top of this document --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we scroll it up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. See, it is coming from the a group calling itself crisis committee in the municipality on Bosanski Novi, which is in Bosnia and Herzegovina. [Indiscernible] -- it is at a different place. The addressee of this memo is myself, who is in the United Nations Protected Area. There was not -- it was a small difference to them. It is no problem. Notwithstanding that, we have nothing to do with Bosanski Novi. But we were in Dvor, which is now, if you scroll down, on the memo, the paragraph that counsel read, you will see one other sentence after the buses being provided by the companies Kozara Prevoz and Autoprevoz Dvor, the bus company was to come from Dvor. Now, these are people in a different city talking about this being provided in another, yet different, city but because they were all Serbs, didn't seem to be unusual. And by private vehicles and other means of transportation on relation in Dvor-Vrginmost-Topusko, that is the route they were supposed to take. And then that paragraph, "Safeguarding" should really have been translated into "security," "to the convoy will be provided by internal affairs of Republic of Serbian Krajina." In short, they would have to -- this was information being given to us that they intend to do this and they were going to do it along those lines. Fast-forward, it took place exactly as they had described it, with buses provided the same way, and there was Toso Paic and all his police representing the internal affairs, manning the route.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can I move, please, this document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit number 754, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to display 65 ter document 844. If we managed to have -- shouldn't be -- I hope that I didn't state it wrong. I apologise. I apologise. I stated a wrong 65 ter. It is 845. On the screen we have B/C/S version and now we have English version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This document is dated 8 of July, and it is issued by Republic of Serbian Krajina Dvor Na Uni Assembly municipal Crisis Staff. And it says, "At session on 7 July 1992, the Dvor Na Uni municipal Crisis Staff discussed a memo from the Bosanski Novi municipal Crisis Staff" - and the number, if we compare this -- these two documents, we would see that the previous one had the same reference number - "concerning voluntary departure of people of Muslims and other ethnicities from the territory of the Bosanski Novi municipality." Have you seen this document?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Are you -- if we go to Article 3, "The Dvor Na Uni public security station is instructed to step up controls of the crossing from the Bosanski Novi to Dvor Na Uni municipality in order to prevent the passage of people of Muslim and other ethnicities and which -- to the departure from the territory of Bosanski Novi municipality." To your knowledge, and you already mentioned it, was police from Dvor Na Uni involved in the transfer of these people from Bosanski Novi to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only the police in Dvor, but all along the route, that took them from Dvor through -- if you look at the map, the route they would have followed would bring them to Vojnic, from Vojnic through Vrginmost. They were all involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you also mentioned that Toso Paic was involved. Can you briefly tell us in which way?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said -- I also used the term "fast-forward," because this was the preparatory stages. All this document was preparatory to the movement. And I said when the movement actually occurred, it went in as the memo had said it would, and Mr. Paic was the regional commissioner of police, as I mentioned his title, his capacity; and he was also the Deputy Minister of Interior. There were several elements that were of concern to the so-called Republic of Srpska Krajina which was to ensure that this number, these many Muslims who were going to cross from Bosanski Novi, they would not kind of remain or disappear into the territory controlled by the Serbs and, of course, become a source of a problem. So they had to ensure that they passed through and nobody stopped in there. That was the intention. No one would stop there. And the last element of all of this, they had to be an agreement between the Croatian government that this group can transition the sector, but, more importantly, they will end up in turn next to Karlovac where the Croatian authority would have the burden of taking care of all these -- the original number was 4.000, double the number actually crossed. So on both sides of this thing, there was a concern both from the Serb side and on the Croatian side, all elements had to be in place before the movement would take place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I think it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Richterova. We will take a break and come back to quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender into evidence the document which we were discussing before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit 755, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, before the break my question was about the involvement of Toso Paic and the police. Based on what you observed, did Toso Paic and police of Republic of Serbian Krajina help to facilitate the movement of Muslims from Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness another document. It's 65 ter 2021.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Before this document is displayed, I want to ask you, after this initial transfer of Muslims -- we have now the document in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you scroll it down, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Is it yours?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we go to the page 2?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This memorandum is dated 13 of August, 1992. Subject: Status of refugees, attempt to cross through Sector North. Did you prepare this memorandum?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I didn't manage to finish my question. After this initial movement of Muslims across the border to Croatia, was there another attempt to move additional Muslims? But can we be very brief? I would read you a small passage from this memorandum. I'm starting in the middle. You met with the representative of UNHCR, the name is mentioned in this document, to discuss the approach to be taken on the new wave of refugees wishing to transit through Sector North, as today the estimate has shot up to 28.000. And then I want to skip one sentence and continue. "To do so would be to participate directly in the process of ethnic cleansing unleashed by the Serbs in Bosnia." Do you remember that you wrote this information about the number of potential refugees in this memorandum?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember, and this memorandum was a case of our prediction coming true, when in the initial stage we were not listened to and the first round of removal of refugees took place. We told them, having achieved that, you just opened the doors. This would be round one. There will be round two and so forth. And this awful practice of ethnic cleansing, unless you do something about it, will now be in full swing. This is the gist of my discussion with the gentlemen who headed UNHCR named in paragraph 2. They -- and I gave them the numbers of 28.000, they were not all from Bosanski Novi. They were supposed to come from a wider -- the numbers added to 28.000, but they were collected from points along northern Bosnia, points such as Bosanska Krupa, Bosanska, Sanski Most, Kljuc. All of these areas had their own estimates. It had begun to gather momentum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I interrupt?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Am I to understand that the practice is not to show documents with names of UNHCR personnel? Am I -- is that -- do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No. The practice is that documents which would be provided by UNHCR shouldn't be displayed in court or used. This document was provided by -- by UNPROFOR, I'm sorry, by UNPROFOR. Out of caution, I didn't mention the name of the representative, but it's true that in fact this document is displayed. So if there is any chance that this part would be -- or the document would be -- would -- I would like to tender this document into evidence, if it could be tendered under seal. And if the part of the tape could be also redacted, which shows the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It doesn't look like the transcript shows the name, but the document does.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yeah, the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much. We will then ask that where the name was broadcast, it be deleted from the transcript. Thank you so much. You are not yet making your application to tender this into evidence? You will still make an application later?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I can -- if I may, I can make this application now and continue with my questioning, not to forget to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then the document is admitted into evidence under seal. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 756, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Okay. You may proceed, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We were talking about your discussions with the representatives of UNHCR. Did really this movement of certain amount or huge amount of Muslims materialise during the remaining part of the year?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm happy to say that after the first movement of refugees, our message began to hold and be the line that was taken not just by the UN but the UNHCR itself, that there shall be no more of these movements. And this attempt did not take place, involving these numbers shown in paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did it happen, however, that people would be still leaving Bosnia and entering either Sector North or any parts of Croatian area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Incidents of small numbers of people, Muslims, as well as -- yeah, mostly Muslims continued to cross the sector, but not in this kind of organised way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to now move in time, and I will ask another document to be displayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just ask, the Muslims who moved in small numbers, did they move voluntarily or were they still moving under pressure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were moving mostly under pressure -- actually they were the true escapees from a problem and were crossing the River Una, because that's where they hoped to find some refuge. But for many of them it wasn't a refuge because they were moving from one Serb-controlled area to another; and when they got into the sector, often it became our responsibility to whisk them to wherever we could find safety for them, usually meaning across to the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the pressure that you seem to be talking about is the pressure that's different from the one where a voluntary move was being organised which was not voluntary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was simply the groups themselves running away and finding their way to our sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And these that are talked about in this document, the 28.000, were they also leaving under that kind of -- which kind of pressure were they leaving under?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This one was a lot more subtle because some of them had been convinced that having been offered these impossible choices they were actually going to take the choices and leave as long as they were safe to leave, The organised ones. To the extent that the names of those who wished to transition had been collected in the second round, the round here -- at one time they brought me a printed computer list containing all the names of the people who had "signed on," to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So in fact, can it be deduced therefore from what you are saying that the phrase, refugees "wishing" to transit, wishing is in quotes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Thank you very much. You may proceed, Ms. Richterova. You want a new document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to have document 854, 65 ter exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, we you -- we can see on this cover page, a name, P. Raffone. Can you tell us who he was?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A man on my civil affairs staff, there was one named Paul -- Paolo Raffone. And given the kind of hectic days we had, where I'm not always where I'm supposed to be for purposes of transmitting documents, he would call me on the telephone, we would finalise the document itself, and then I will give him authorisation to release it. This is one instant.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we go to page 2?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This document is dated 20th of July, 1992, and it is: "Periodic overall reports." This document is quite a lengthy. Can we -- and it is signed -- is it correct that it is signed by you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document prepared, as because of its length, with the full resources of my office, but is one that I take the responsibility, not only for its content but for its release.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we go now to page 12? The last four digits in the ERN number -- yes, should be 2261. Can we scroll down? More, please. So we can see what is under this local authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Here it says, "Almost all the mayors of the seven opstinas of Sector North were appointed when the Croatian authorities pulled out of the territory during the autumn of 1991. The only mayor who served both before and after the conflict was Mr. Obradovic of Vrginmost. He was assassinated recently on the road, about two kilometres from Topusko." Can you please briefly tell us something about, first about Mr. Obradovic? For example, what was his view of implementation of the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had alluded to it, to that matter, in an earlier question today, when I said the views of the mayors ranged from those who didn't give any -- and I mentioned his name - and those who gave very, very passionate views about the future. Mr. Obradovic, of whom I had the pleasure of meeting so many times, was the kind who did what he thought the Vance Plan required. He didn't talk about it much; he just did it. He also tried to -- to be the mayor as envisaged in the Vance Plan, not referring to any overarching authority, meaning you -- I never would hear him talking about the Serbian Republic of Krajina in Knin or anything. All matters were within the mayoral responsibilities. He was also rather efficient in doing what he did. That was -- and he did it quietly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In this report, you mentioned that he was assassinated. What do you know about the circumstances or what followed after his assassination? Was there any investigation?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one of those traumatic events, as the paragraph says, it's only two kilometres from where we were. I recall it might have been Saturday morning. The area where his house was located is rather wooded, kind of -- you drive for a kilometre in a completely wooded part of that. That's where he was waylaid. His car was well known - it was red and you couldn't miss it - it was sprayed with bullets, and he was immediately taken to a local hospital. I was also immediately called by his colleagues, including Mile Paspalj and others. When I arrived in the hospital, they were there. The reason I was asked to join them is if I could provide them with a med evacuation, helicopters to evacuate him, to a better hospital. He was still in surgery when I arrived. What was interesting was that it was a charged atmosphere. The local people were literally terrified. Mr. Paspalj packed a gun, which he normally -- Mile Paspalj, he normally wouldn't wear. He was packing a gun. There was an element of fear about -- all among them, not explainable by just the assassination. We couldn't give them what they wanted because when I said -- when they asked me, Could we evacuate him to a better hospital, the answer was Yes. And the nearest -- we have a helicopter. The nearest we will evacuate you is Zagreb. They refused flatly, saying, "We should evacuate them all the way to Belgrade." That was, of course, not a viable option, nor was it being considered on basis of medicine; it was being considered for other reasons other than medicine. Anyway, the debate became moot because by 1.30, while we are still talking in the anteroom to the operation room, the doctor came and said he had died. Immediately there was the usual panic about who killed him, with some speculation that -- of how he might have been killed. None of the usual rhetoric that I heard was present in this case, because if he had been killed by the parties to the conflict on the other side, meaning Croats, I would immediately have heard, it would have been condemned that the Croats came and committed assassination here. We didn't hear that. Secondly, the entire route within those two kilometres was fully manned with the -- with the -- the armed Serb people at the junction of the road between Glina and Vrginmost, there was a junction control manned by the military. And you couldn't commit that crime and run away. Anyway, nobody was ever arrested or ever charged with the crime of killing Obradovic. When I asked for it, not a single person in or outside of the authorities wished to discuss it. They were all apprehensive of the very question, Can you tell me who killed Mr. Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we now turn to following page, please? It's page 13.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will concentrate on the first paragraph. "Prior to the assassination of Mayor Obradovic, we observed two parallel lines of politics and control. The Milicija on one side appeared to be getting direct instructions from Knin; the mayors, on the other hand, seem to exercise a measure of political autonomy depending on the opstina. Some mayors have told us that the chiefs of the local police were not informing them about their activities." After the assassination of Mr. Obradovic, was there any change in these two parallel lines?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were completely the absence of anyone who would even venture an opinion that was not aligned to what was perceived to be the correct opinion or policy coming from Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you say "correct opinion or policy coming from Knin," what do you --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean no one would exercise any kind of independence similar to what Obradovic seemed to exhibit or not to be obviously singing the line from Knin. They all began now to talk about whether the republic of Serbian Krajina and their government in Knin. They were kind of all aligned, and some were also changed. The mayor of Vojnic, for example, was changed. Some police or some police chiefs -- I don't remember exactly where that might have happened, but the mayor of Vojnic is a case where we had a change.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we now please go to page 5 of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What would page 5 be?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Page 5 of the document which is displayed. I started from the backward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. My pages end at 2263. Is -- would that be it?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, it is 2254.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You already discussed that in fact during your work you had to discuss certain issues with both sides, Croatian side and Serb side. This part refers to your discussions with Croats, and it says, "Protection of Croats in the UNPAs." And it says that, "The Croatian commissioners have supplied a list of over 1.700 persons left behind in the UNPA and over 22.000 said to be displaced or missing," and then there is a breakdown. What we are seeing now on the screen, is it a something what you prepared or is it something what you were provided by the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something that was provided by the Croatian side, and taking off your comment about our discussion on the Croatian side, I would like to specifically to add that on the Croatian side, they had mirrored -- like shadow, mayors and shadow police who had been within the sector and were forced to move out of the sector. They were concentrated either in Karlovac or Sisak. Organisationally they were led by the Deputy Prime Minister, Dr. Ramljak who'd chaired them when they met as the shadow mayors of Slunj, Vojnic and all of that. And each time I went into that room, it was -- it was a very hot room because it was full of people, angry, and, of course, very concerned about what happened in the sector. They had at this point in time begun to focus on what they called Croats left behind when they themselves took to refuge across the confrontation line. The question to me was, How are they doing? Are they protected or are the Serbs terrorising them? In answer to all those questions was, I don't know, because I don't know who is left behind, and I don't know where they are, because we don't go looking for them as Croats. So they gave me a list saying, We think you can find so many, like 352 in Slunj - and the number is shown on the screen - this is what we expect you should be finding. We had a long discussion with the government, Dr. Ramljak as the Deputy Prime Minister. And I told them that I would like them to make a choice. Some of these people, the fact that we don't know, the anonymity may be the only reason they are protected. If you identified them -- we had seen incidents, particularly around Glina opstina, where if they were identified as Croats they were subjects of attacks, and some had been murdered, there were several murders there. So will you, the government, make a choice? If you ask you us to go looking for them, the consequence of identifying them will also be loss of protection by anonymity which they enjoyed. They took some time to think about it, and they decided they will take the responsibility and therefore I should accept this list and go back to the sector and account for either their presence or absence. That's the context in which this is presented.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we -- can I move this document into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it will be Exhibit 757.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will continue with line of question -- my questioning about Croats left behind, but before I do it I would like to show you one document. It is 65 ter 856. Did you write this cover page?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also recognise this to be done similarly on my behalf, not my handwriting but on my behalf.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we now go to page 3?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And this is a document dated 21st of July, 1992, and it is meeting with Mr. Spanovic, and he's identified here as a Defence Minister of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. In fact, this document refers to what you said before, under -- if we can --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we scroll down, please? More.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Local police and Milicija. It refers to: "Our discussions on local police matters centred on three unresolved murders of Croatians in Glina and two others in Slunj. We explained to him that while the attitude of civilian authorities against the perpetrators of the crimes was admirable, the progress of the local police seems slow." Do you know whether -- anything about the progress of the investigation of these murders?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was always assured that they were being done to the best of their abilities. As of this day, I don't recall this investigation being brought to an end and a suspect being charged or convicted for any of the murders.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we go now to page 3 -- I'm sorry, 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The first paragraph says, "Mr. Spanovic took note of the details of the cases and promised a swift solution. He also repeated that Knin authorities should be informed of problems such as this." Who did he refer to as authorities in Knin? Which authorities should have been informed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this instant, I was the intermediary between the Croatian authorities led by the Deputy Prime Minister, and the Serbs representing Serbian Krajina, led by Colonel Spanovic. He was a colonel, and he was the Defence Minister. When the Croats took the position that all of these people must be identified, it was also requested of me that I take each of the lists that they had prepared and officially and formally present it to both the mayor and chief of police of each of the opstinas. That was done. But because they were presented by that official request through me from the government of Croats -- of the Croatian -- they also replied in kind, that they needed a decision by the government of Krajina. When Colonel Spanovic was talking to me, since he was himself a government member, in fact, he wore the title the Defence Minister, he was talking about discussing it with broad -- I assume the cabinet, if there was a cabinet meeting over there. Anyway, whatever it is they discussed, the result was an answer as to the policy they would follow about this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we scroll down, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We have return of displaced persons. You already mentioned yesterday that it was one of the features of the Vance Plan, the voluntary return of displaced persons. If we look to the first paragraph under the heading, "Return of displaced persons." In the middle it says, "Mr. Spanovic said his government would be guided by regulations passed in Knin on return of refugees. Today he sent me an English version of the regulations."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we now go to page 2?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Could you have a look at this decision, if we could scroll down a little bit? This document was dated April 21st, 1992. Yes. Thank you. Did you -- do you remember seeing this document at the time when you wrote this report?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If we could look to -- yes, under Article 2, it -- this document is showing how to -- what is necessary to do when someone wants to return; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And it says, "Upon the reception of the written request of the persons asking for the return, permission within 90-day long deadline, the Secretariat of Internal Affairs is incumbent on carrying out the verification of the eventual collaboration, direct or indirect, in the enemy forces or the nationalist, fascist parties that used to propagate or execute the activities to the damage of Serbian people, which finally entailed the genocide repetition." Did you discuss with Mr. Spanovic this decision and how helpful the decision it is for the return of refugees?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I'm -- I want to say I had very good cooperative relationship with Colonel Spanovic. In most of the issues that I engaged him, he did produce some result, not always satisfactory, but he did. He was a soldier. This is a civilian matter involving legislation. We knew, both him and I, when I looked at it, particularly paragraph 2. I spoke earlier on the constant refrain from Serbian mayors and others, we can't live together with the Serbs and Croats. Secondly, they all knew the provisions of the Vance Plan, that the right by the signatories of that document was given to all parties to return to their homes with no such conditions. So I read it as they finally had figured a way of actually preventing or making it impossible for anyone to return by the conditions that they outlined in paragraph 2, where every Croat -- very few of them would escape the clause, that they were collaboration with the enemy forces or with the nationalist, fascist parties that used to propagate those -- that paragraph was a catch-all paragraph that would have actually denied the very thing it purports to enable. We didn't take it seriously, in the sense that it would permit any Croats to return. No. We knew it will be used as the reason for not allowing them to return.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can I move this document into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit 758, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Another document I would like to display is 65 ter 863. Can we go, please, to page 3?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This document is dated 8 of August, 1992. Do you remember this document as the one you prepared?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If we could scroll down a little bit, there is a local Milicija.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It says, "Series of meetings with the commanders of the local Milicija have been held. The sector commander has firmly impressed on the Milicija that the switch of personnel from TDF" -- you said it's Territorial Defence forces; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: -- "to the Milicija or special police forces is not acceptable. The personnel have to be completely demobilised." Does it reflect the situation as it was in the Sector North in August, that there were still personnel which was switching to the Milicija?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we go to page 4?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Under Article 4, "The local Milicija disagreed, however, with the Vance Plan requirement that they carry only side-arms, as well as UNPROFOR insistence that they discard all military camouflage uniforms, which some of them still wear, with a Milicija arm-band." Does it reflect the situation in -- still in August in the area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you are talking -- when you are talking here about this Milicija arm-band, do you remember how it looked like?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The insignia of the Milicija was always in blue with some coat of arms and some inscription which was invariably in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Is it a please possible -- I will return back to this document or maybe we can place one document on the ELMO. It is already court Exhibit 266.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing this arm-band?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it's a familiar sight.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Is it the one you are referring to in this document?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we now return back to the document 863? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This same article continues, "The local commanders cited the following in support of their dissent." And we don't need to read all these four -- four or how many -- subarticles, but we -- I would like to read you subarticle or subparagraph (d). "The special police, Milicija, does not fall within the command structure of the normal Milicija. They operate mostly in camouflage uniforms and have most of the assault rifles. They are commanded by two separate individuals, one each for Banija and Kordun, and report directly to Mr. Martic in Knin." Is it how the local commanders saw the situation?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You might have heard me refer to this very thing very early, when you asked me, Your Honour, about the switch of uniform. I said over time they also switched back and put these Milicijas in the border or the so-called border with -- of the RSK. I specifically also mentioned that the -- at the beginning the first group was commanded out of Slunj and commanded by Colonel Novakovic; and the second group was centred in Banija under Colonel Tarbuk. They all wore green, not blue, and they were in certain ways a lot more powerful than the Milicija in blue uniform. And as this paragraph indicates, since this was an interior matter, the person who ran the interior affairs was Mr. Martic, and they were beholden to Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can I move this document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit 759, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can document 871 be displayed? 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Is this document submitted by you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we go to page 2?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This document is dated 26 of September, 1992. It's civil affairs sitrep, and under Article 2, it says, "It is a common perception among the Serbian leadership here that the provision in SCR, Security Council Resolution, 762, requiring the restoration of Croatian authority in the pink zones was a betrayal of their cause." And before I ask you a question, I would like to go to page 5. And the subheading is: "Demobilisation of the Special Milicija," and if we could go, scroll down. Mr. Kirudja, if you could have a look at paragraph 11, and make a comment regarding this demobilisation of the special Milicija? What was the situation? How did they see it? And is it correct, as we saw at the beginning, that this is referring to the pink zone?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, counsel. I took the opportunity when I was tracing the pink zones at the very beginning to mention that they became a subject of a special Security Council resolution, and I also mentioned they required that the Croatian authority be restored. I didn't use restoration, but I said that their control should be returned sooner, and -- irrespective of the UNPA. Yes, that paragraph refers to that resolution and its effect. On paragraph 11, we were still trying to accomplish the demobilisation that was called for by the Vance Plan elsewhere in the rest of the UNPA. This -- because of the time it took to accomplish it, events had formed on the ground creating this issue of the special Milicija that I just described that used to start -- in the -- in the borders, and then the order came. The negotiations were being done for a demobilisation and laying down of the arms, and because of the protracted nature of those negotiations, they couldn't be done sector by sector. So the mission approached the matter from the top, that the terms of whatever is agreed by the Serbs will apply to all the sectors. In order for that to be practical, it involved an agreement reached between the force commander and Mr. Martic. Mr. Martic -- and mainly because at that point he had total control of these forces. Therefore, to demobilise them, they had to reach agreement with the force commander, and that agreement was then communicated to each of the sectors, including our sector. This is what is in reference to. And there was a meeting where the local commanders, both in Kordun, Banija, gathered to hear the terms of this demobilisation. That's what the reference is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I asked you at the beginning, was -- did it refer to specifically to demilitarisation of the pink zones?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The pink zones were to be treated under the terms of the Resolution 762. There was by nature -- because it's on the front line, you have to think of it how the front line looks like. There is an area on both sides, about two or three kilometres, which is an approachable for all kinds of reasons, because of either mining or because it is very hostile area, but the pink zones also carried beyond the area that you would know as confrontation zones, as you saw there, and take a whole chunk of an area into the control of the Serbs. That is the areas which had not been named by the Vance Plan. The resolution 762 restored that request by the Croatian government that we are not going to wait for the Vance Plan to play out. The Security Council agreed. You, UNPROFOR, are to do what you have to do to restore the Croatian authorities in those areas, and then you get on with the Vance Plan as originally conceived.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to move this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 760, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to display document 851. And it looks that in the e-court it should be under 851A and 851B. 851, just -- I can see this production list, so let's hope that the whole document is in the e-court. Can we go to page 2? There should be another page which is ZA022270.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We are now in the subject of the treatment of Croats. This memorandum, did you prepare it? It's dated 16 of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And the subject is: "The five Croats from Sector South now in Park Hotel Slunj." What happened to these five Croats?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, a quick summary how they got there. They were not originally from Sector North. They were from somewhere in Korenica in Sector South, where they had been expelled from their houses by some Milicija in Korenica. I can't tell you the details, other than they showed up on their way out in Slunj, where they were accommodated into a hotel by the mayor and his chief of police, and we are talking about mayor of Slunj, Babic -- or what is his name? I'll see it in a minute there, and his chief of police, Mr. Klipe [phoen]. That one doesn't come readily into to my head. I never --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If we scroll down, we can see the name of the mayor in Slunj, if you could read it.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosic -- Bosnjic, yeah, that's the mayor, Bosnjic. And they -- to my -- it was kind of unusual surprise that they did something that I wasn't used to seeing, and which I hoped would happen more often, because the mayor and his chief undertook to house these Croats at a great risk which he spoke to me about, and he spoke to me about it saying, "I will only be able to keep them there for a while, while you find a solution to what we, UNPROFOR, found a solution what to do with these five Croats. There they were ordinary people. These were not people involved in any particular thing; they were just ordinary folks that had been thrown out of their house.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What happened to them? Did they -- were they able to return or did they stay in Slunj or did they end up elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eventually, they were removed from the sector, but under circumstances where the Croats themselves facilitated that, but I won't get to the circumstances because it happened later after the Medak attack. The Croats now were sure that whatever Croats were around there might be subjected to a back-lash so they were removed much later, but for a very long time, they were in the hotel in Slunj.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In connection with these five Croats, did you try to communicate with Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And that's what I was trying to get at, because when Mr. Bosnjic approached me he was very concerned that as mayor, as well as the chief of police, the very act, the humane act of keeping them in a hotel was a problem for him. And I said to him, "Under the terms of this, that's your government. They were chased out of another part. The only solution is to take them back to their home." He said, "I can't do that, but they are here and I can't continue using public funds," which they were using, "to keep them in the hotel." And the hint was he would get into trouble with Knin. Knin was in that case -- since this is a police statement, Mr. Martic was the Minister of Interior. All the security of everybody, ordinary people -- if you are a Minister of Interior you're responsible for the plight of everybody. So I wrote to them saying, I wrote to Mr. Martic to say to him, "These people are here. They are being -- they are being taken care of. We are glad they are being taken care of by the mayor, and we think it's up to your authorities to complete this matter and return these people to the safety of their own house."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what happened? Did he reply?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was it the first letter or first communication which you sent to Mr. Martic or were there more than one?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember sending more than one or -- or this communication, because on matters that I had to reduce to writing had to come to a certain level of seriousness for me to do so. And I did this because I found out if I wanted a solution, putting things in writing actually wasn't always the best way of finding a solution. I preferred to talk to them and persuade them on a one-to-one basis of something to do. I didn't have that opportunity. Mr. Martic was based in Knin, and I'm based in Topusko and this is happening in my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to move this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. It will be Exhibit 761, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we now display 65 ter 838? Can we go to page 2 -- I'm sorry, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This document is dated 21st of June. If we could scroll down, we would see that this report was prepared by Paolo Raffone, and it talks, "Suspected new expulsion of Croats on the border between Sector North - South." And if we look at the second -- in the second paragraph, there is -- it states that according to one Mr. Hajdukovic, a group of uniformed persons arrived in the village on 19th June, driving a tractor. They entered the house of the 12 Croats and expelled them immediately from their houses. Only four persons are left now in this village. If we could go to page 2. This is signed by you, and it says, it is a self-explanatory report. Based on this, do you remember seeing this report on the page 3?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know about this incident?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an incident that, when Mr. Raffone, as I explained earlier who was one of staff reporting to me, drew to my attention, and the nature of the incident itself, I was afraid it might be the beginning of a bigger pattern where people would be thrown out, if they are Croats, so to make room for other Serbs coming from wherever they came from, including from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, bear in mind that even if a lot of people had been expelled from the sector, there were not too many empty houses because the act of expelling them was also precipitated by destruction of most houses. So accommodation was a precious thing. So in order to accommodate Serbs, who have also been expelled, or reportedly expelled, from Bosnia - because I wasn't in Bosnia to see the act of expulsion - those who came in, like this case wherein they looked at a group of people called Croats and expelled them, was of great concern to me so that it doesn't gather momentum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You talk of people being expelled from the sector. Were they being expelled from the sector?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I wasn't clear. What I meant is that prior to our arrival the expulsion had already been completed in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the sector?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we now go back to page 3? Scroll down a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And it's something what you already mentioned. "They also," referring -- it's paragraph 3, "Polish battalion." "They also confirmed that some days before the reported incident, some houses were burned in Catrnja and Smoljanac." When you travelled in the area, were you aware of any such incident or did you see burned houses, destroyed houses?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, this was almost impossible to distinguish, almost every house you saw was shot, burned, or blown out, one way or the other. If you took a car and drove in any of these towns, you will be impressed by the amount of violence that was visited in every house that you saw. So that if a recent event would occur -- so that whatever house that was left standing is subsequently also fire-bombed or the -- it would make very little difference, you probably not even notice by driving around.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you able to distinguish whether these villages or the houses, who lived in these villages and whose houses were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on which opstina you're talking about, some were readily easy to tell who used to live there, especially, say, in Slunj. A good number of -- a very large number of those who lived in Slunj were Croats who were already gathered in Karlovac, which I mentioned earlier today. A huge number of those who had been forced out of Slunj, I would meet a lot of them in Karlovac. They were Croats. If you go into Vrginmost, some parts of Vrginmost, most villages were left intact because the predominant population there wasn't all Croats, except as you approach the confrontation line. Then the destruction picks up, and that tells you the majority of the people who lived along that area from Tursilovic [phoen] to Turijn [phoen] and along the Mrezinica and Kupa River on the side of the Serb side, most houses had been destroyed. That tells you the occupants mostly were Croats, and the story is repeated that way all over.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can I move this document into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit 762, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we now display document 65 ter 874? Can we go to page 2?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This document is dated 16 October 1992. It's from Mr. Kirudja. Subject: "Urgent measures to ensure the protection of minorities in Glina opstina." I want to refer you to the first paragraph, somewhere in the middle. It says, "Information reaching us recently show, however, a disturbing pattern of abuse, harassment, and discriminatory treatment of Croats, particularly in seven villages south of Glina town." We are now in October, so I would like to talk to you about the situation in the sector around this time, September, October, November. How was the situation, and mainly if we could focus on the treatment of Croats? What did you personally observe?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the result of what I said earlier and is mentioned on the very sentence on this memo, first sentence on paragraph 1, that with agreement of both sides, both the Croatian side and the Serb side, I sent out letters to each of the opstinas telling them there were Croats, or expected Croats, so many in -- in your opstina.
