When this letter arrived in Glina, part of what I was originally concerned began it play out, because now they started focusing on them. And it was also -- even before the letters were sent out, it was also Glina where a lot of hostilities was unleashed, including the murders mentioned earlier on Croats. So this situation became critical enough because those villages which I identified as containing mostly Croats, began to be terrorised, the people there began to get repercussions. We didn't have enough of our protection forces deployed in those villages where this was occurring. So I used -- this memo, I used it to formally request the sector commander to adjust the deployment of the military contingents closer to where these villages were, to give them some relief by the mere presence of UNPROFOR, because there was a constant harassment of the -- of the people in those seven villages, particularly one of them called Maja.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You were still in the area in 1993. Did this pattern of harassment, ill treatment, did it continue in 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1993, the time-line -- I wish I remembered the date because I don't have it ready in my head when Medak attack, the Croats attacked viciously, unexpectedly, with such force a village called Medak. I don't have that date, but it's a watershed date because the reaction of the Serbs was particularly also and expected to have been very -- there was a big back-lash.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: May I interrupt just for a second? To your knowledge, this Medak village, was it in the pink zone?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- probably, but it was in Sector South, that's why I don't have the details. It was not in my sector. But remember, events I said earlier, in all sectors, if they were precipitated events by one side or the other had an affect in all sectors. The effect of Medak was while the Croats were resisting all the time, the pressure for those Croats who wanted because of insecurity to cross over the line -- the conflict and go and join their friends and others, either in Karlovac or Sisak, the Croats would refuse to let them come. But after Medak, they knew they can't maintain that policy, and they opened -- they made it much easier for any Croat who wanted to take refuge across the border. So the numbers of those people who were -- who had -- Croats left behind was suddenly reduced by those who fled after Medak or possible repercussions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to move this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it will be Exhibit 763, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to display another document, and it is 887.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This document is dated 10 of February, 1994. You can see that we move a little bit forward in the time. At this time, you were still in Sector North.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2, a little bit scrolled -- now it's too much. I'm sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In the second paragraph, this document talks about result of the elections that Mr. Martic was elected president. And at the end of this paragraph, it says, "It was against this eventuality that Martic won support of Milosevic against Babic in the recent campaign and won. Now the question is whether or not he, Martic, can govern." Did you follow still -- in the Sector North, did you follow the events -- the elections in Republika --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You made this comment, "support of Milosevic." So how did you -- based on the knowledge of the situation, the political situation, how did you view the result of the elections?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This election was very well publicised. It was -- there was a -- I hasten to call it a campaign. There was a lot of talk about this election, about ballots being printed and reprinted, and it was something that occupied all leaders that we spoke with, about this election. Now, bear in mind it was a contest that pitted Mr. Martic and Mr. Babic, and Mr. Babic's view of this sector -- I started yesterday to mention that from the very beginning, Mr. Babic didn't see eye to eye on Vance Plan. As a matter of fact, he had -- was originally expected to sign that Vance Plan and didn't -- because he didn't like it, he refused to sign it. And instead, Mile Paspalj, the gentleman I spoke about, signed it at the request of Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me. I thought you talked about this a little earlier today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I thought you then said it was Mr. Martic who refused to sign, not Babic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no, it's Babic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's Babic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's Babic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So I must have been --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not Mr. Martic. Now in this context, because Mr. Milosevic had a certain vision of how all this matter should end - I won't go into details, I had occasion to talk to him personally on it so I can summarise - it was not possible for Babic to -- for Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Babic to see eye to eye if he was in charge, if he had won the election. The direction of how all of this will go would not have gone in the direction Mr. Milosevic was envisioning. So this election was fought, and there were a lot of talk about ballots and no ballots, but in the end he won. And my surmising was that he won because he had the support from Belgrade this -- and that's what I said, "support of Milosevic" on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What -- what do you read into -- you mentioned twice now. You said, there were printing and reprinting of papers, and then you said there were ballots and not ballots. What do you read into that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got the idea that there was a lot of contest about whether -- how the voting went locally. We were -- we had no role to participate in it, so we were just watchers of what was going on. And I was hearing there were not enough ballots here. They have sent new ballots there. That sort of thing. In an election when you're hearing about ballots being printed, sent here and there, you know what, it can always mean a whole lot of things.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: A question following is: Do you know where these ballots were printed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Went -- without saying everything, that was in support of this UNPA was being done from Belgrade. Though I didn't see them actually being printed, it would have been hard to imagine they were being printed in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can see that it's already a little bit after 7.00, and I will start a new area and it will -- it won't take very long, tomorrow of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Richterova. It is 7.00 or actually five past 7.00. We are going to adjourn and we will carry on tomorrow at quarter past 2.00. Tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the same courtroom. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 1st day of June, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.04 p.m.,
